ladwp:cc-r-1b-2026-04-01: One rate element on the published Schedule R-1(B) summary sheet is not represented in this filing: the Electric Vehicle Discount, shown as -$0.02500 per kWh in both the High Season (June through September) and Low Season (October through May) columns, immediately beneath the three time-of-use energy charges it adjusts. Everything else on the sheet is modeled: the $12.00 monthly Service Charge, the six energy charges (High Peak, Low Peak and Base in each season), and the seven per-kWh adjustment factors (ECA, ESA, RCA, VEA, CRPSEA, VRPSEA and IRCA). The discount is conditional and the summary sheet does not say on what; its only footnote reads "Conditions for this element set in the capped ordinance". That ordinance, Schedule R-1 Section 4.b, supplies the eligibility test: owners of licensed passenger electric vehicles, on proof of vehicle registration and charging location. It does not publish the quantity, stating only that the discount applies to "the block of energy designated by the Department as necessary for basic vehicle charging", so a consumer cannot derive the discounted quantity from the tariff at all. A consumer billing an electric-vehicle owner on R-1(B) will therefore compute a charge that is too high by 2.5 cents per kWh on that block. The sheet's eligibility narrative is modeled, as is its mandatory-service rule: customers whose annual monthly average consumption reaches or exceeds 3,000 kWh in the preceding 12 months must take service under Rate B, and a customer who transfers off Rate B may not revert for 12 months.
ladwp:cc-ez-save-2008-09-01: The source ordinance states this subsidy as a complete rate rather than as a credit line, and this filing models only the credit. Schedule R-1 Section 2.d, Rate D Low Income Service, sets it at "Rate A less $8.17, ESA, and RCA" effective July 1, 2009, and Section 3 Billing repeats the same three-part construction. The filing carries the $8.17 per month (published by LADWP as $16.34 every two months and modeled here as -$0.2683 per meter-day) but not the accompanying waiver of the two per-kWh adjustments: the Electric Subsidy Adjustment and the Reliability Cost Adjustment, $0.00147 and $0.00300 per kWh on the current residential rate sheets, survive on the base plan when this modifier is applied, so a bill computed from base plan plus modifier overstates an EZ-Save customer's charges by their sum on every kWh. Two smaller points of fidelity. The credit is published per two-month billing period and modeled per day at the 60.875-day average, so a customer on a longer or shorter cycle receives a credit slightly away from the published figure. LADWP's residential rates page adds that the subsidy is not to exceed the customer's bill; that floor is not modeled, and binds only where a bill is smaller than the credit. Note also that the ordinance frames Rate D as a variant of Rate A, the standard non-time-of-use service, while this filing offers the credit as a modifier applicable to both R-1(A) and R-1(B). Eligibility is out of scope rather than missing: Section 4.a.(4) states no income test in the tariff, deferring the requirements to the Board of Water and Power Commissioners and to guidelines published off-tariff, so the filing tests enrollment in the program instead.
ladwp:cc-lifeline-2008-09-01: Three provisions of Schedule R-1's Lifeline Service are not represented, and the eligibility rule is narrower than the tariff's. Section 5.a.(4) escalates the credit for customers who qualify more than once: a customer eligible in two of the three criteria categories receives 150 percent of the Lifeline Credit, and one eligible in all three receives 175 percent. This filing models a single value, the base $17.71 per month (published as $35.42 every two months and modeled as -$0.5817 per meter-day), so a multiply-qualifying customer's credit is understated by half or by three-quarters again. Section 2.e sets a Minimum Charge of $2.00 for Rate E and Section 3 Billing makes it a floor, the bill being Rate A less the Lifeline Credits "but not less than the Minimum Charge"; no floor is modeled. Sections 2.e and 3 also strike the ESA and RCA per-kWh adjustments ($0.00147 and $0.00300 per kWh on the current residential rate sheets) along with the credit, which this filing does not do, so both charges survive on a bill computed from base plan plus modifier. On eligibility, Section 5.a enumerates three qualifying paths: a senior citizen or disabled individual eligible for exemption from the City Utility Users Tax, a resident who regularly requires an essential life-support device, and a physician-certified allowance for a named set of conditions or a compromised immune system. None of the three is an income test, and the filing collapses all of them into one enrollment predicate described in terms of age or disability plus income guidelines, which loses the distinction the 150 and 175 percent escalation depends on. Deliberately out of scope: the duty in Section 5.a.(4) to notify LADWP when eligibility ends, and the back-billing of up to 36 months plus interest that follows a failure to notify, are enrollment compliance procedures rather than rate structure.
ladwp:cc-nem-2008-09-01: The rider's central number is absent. Service Rider NEM Section 3.b compensates excess exported energy using "the applicable Rate Schedule energy pricing", meaning whatever energy charge the customer's own base schedule carries for the tier, period and season in question, and this filing ships a placeholder credit of zero in its place. URPX v0.5.1 requires a price reference to resolve to a price stated in the same document, so a filing cannot say "the energy charge of whichever plan this customer is on" (urpx-org/urpx discussion 34). A consumer must compute the credit from the customer's own R-1(A) or R-1(B) prices, and the zero here must not be read as zero-value export. Two further billing provisions survive only as descriptive prose, and a third is absent altogether. Section 3.b suspends, in any period where generation exceeds consumption, all charges "based upon kWh" and not the energy charge alone, which on the current residential schedules also drops the ECA, ESA, RCA, VEA, CRPSEA, VRPSEA and IRCA adjustments; the filing's prose narrows this to the energy charges, and nothing in its structure conditions any of those charges on net flow. Section 3.c rolls a credit balance forward to later bills, excluding Taxes and Minimum Charges, and zeroes any remaining balance at termination of service with no further compensation. Section 3.d, which confines a credit balance to the bill for the meter that recorded the excess energy, appears nowhere in the filing, neither in structure nor in prose; a consumer aggregating credits across a multi-meter premises would be wrong to do so and nothing here says otherwise. The eligibility rule carries the rider's applicability conditions in its description but tests only three in structured form (on-site solar, wind or hybrid generation, bidirectional metering, and the one-megawatt cap), so the parallel-operation, own-load-offset, interconnection-cost and signed-interconnection-agreement conditions, and the exclusion of customers on Schedules CG-2 and CG-3, cannot be evaluated automatically. Out of scope rather than missing: Sections 2.b and 2.c allocate the cost of atypical or additional meters and Section 1.a reserves the final applicability determination to the Department, all administrative rather than rate provisions, and Section 2.d's option to buy Green Power is a separate rider, Service Rider REO.
